System Design Principles for Retrieval-Augmented Systems

KEEP THE RETRIEVAL PATH SIMPLE

The retrieval path is on the critical path of every user query. Every added
component (query rewriter, multi-query expander, hypothetical document
embedder) adds latency and a failure mode. Add complexity only when you can
measure an improvement on your eval harness. Resist the urge to add every
technique from every paper.

SEPARATE BUILD TIME FROM QUERY TIME

Expensive operations — embedding generation, index construction, parent
document storage, contextual header generation — belong at ingestion time,
not query time. At query time you want to: embed the query once, search once
or twice, rerank once, and return. Everything else is technical debt against
your latency budget.

MEASURE BEFORE OPTIMIZING

Instrument your pipeline with wall-clock timings at each stage: embedding,
vector search, keyword search, neighbor expansion, reranking, LLM generation.
Optimization without instrumentation means guessing. Guessing is expensive.

PREFER IDEMPOTENT INGESTION

Ingestion pipelines should be safe to run multiple times on the same document.
Use a content hash (SHA-256 of the raw file) to detect unchanged documents
and skip re-embedding. This makes reruns safe and avoids duplicate chunks in
the vector store.

DESIGN FOR FILTERING FROM DAY ONE

Multi-tenant retrieval systems need per-user document isolation from the
start. Adding user_id filters to vector and keyword search after the fact
requires index changes and schema migrations. If you know users will have
private documents, add user_id as a filter parameter at the schema design
stage.

FAIL LOUDLY IN RETRIEVAL, GRACEFULLY IN GENERATION

If the retriever returns zero results, return an empty context to the LLM
and let it say it doesn't know — do not silently pass an empty string that
causes the LLM to hallucinate. On the generation side, graceful degradation
is acceptable: a partial answer is better than an error response.

GOLDEN SETS ARE EXPENSIVE, USE THEM WISELY

A manually annotated golden set of 50-100 queries with relevance judgments
takes significant time to build. Once built, it is one of the most valuable
artifacts in the project. Never auto-generate relevance labels without human
review. Store the golden set in version control alongside the code.

AVOID EMBEDDING MODEL LOCK-IN

Your embedding dimension is baked into the vector schema. Switching models
requires re-embedding the entire corpus and migrating the index. Choose a
model that fits your accuracy, latency, and cost requirements before going
to production. If you must switch later, plan for a dual-model transition
period where both old and new embeddings coexist.

CHUNK SIZE IS A HYPERPARAMETER

The chunk size that works for a dense technical manual is not the same as
the chunk size that works for short news articles. Tune chunk_size and
chunk_overlap on your actual corpus using your golden set. A few percentage
points of Recall@5 can be won or lost on this single decision.

CONTEXT WINDOW BUDGETING

The LLM has a finite context window. Retrieved chunks compete with the system
prompt, conversation history, and the generated answer for space. Calculate
your worst-case token usage: if the system prompt is 2000 tokens, conversation
history is 3000, and each chunk is 512, then passing 10 chunks leaves no room
for a meaningful answer. Pick a top-K that fits.
